guide.title: Chest Pain & Acute Coronary Syndrome
guide.lead: Time is muscle. Get a 12-lead in the first 10 minutes, give aspirin and treat the pain. If it's a STEMI, go straight to a PCI centre. Before nitrates, check the BP, the right ventricle and the bathroom cabinet.

steps.title: 12-lead ECG
steps.text: Within 10 minutes of reaching the patient; transmit and repeat if the pain changes.

steps.title: Aspirin
steps.text: Non-enteric, chewed, unless truly allergic or actively bleeding.

steps.title: Oxygen only if needed
steps.text: SpO₂ below 90% or short of breath. Routine oxygen doesn't help.

steps.title: Destination
steps.text: STEMI: straight to a PCI-capable centre with pre-notification. Aim for first contact to device in 90 minutes or less.

sections.title: Nitrates: check first
include: IV access ready if your protocol requires it
exclude: Systolic BP below 90 mmHg; heart rate below 50/min
Inferior STEMI until V4R rules out RV infarction

quiz.q: Inferior STEMI. After nitroglycerin, BP falls from 128/78 to 72/40. Most likely cause?
options: Right ventricular infarction: nitrates dropped the preload it depends on
quiz.explanation: Record V4R before nitrates in inferior STEMI; give fluid for hypotension per protocol.

quiz.q: When should the first 12-lead be done in chest pain?
options: Within 10 minutes of reaching the patient
Only if the pain lasts over an hour

quiz.q: Nitroglycerin dose for ischemic chest pain:
options: 0.4 mg sublingual every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses

quiz.q: A patient took tadalafil 30 hours ago. Nitroglycerin?
options: No: tadalafil within 48 hours rules it out
Yes: it's been more than 24 hours
Only if BP is above 90 mmHg
quiz.explanation: Sildenafil and vardenafil: 24 hours. Tadalafil: 48 hours.

quiz.q: Oxygen in suspected ACS is indicated when:
options: SpO₂ is below 90% or the patient is short of breath
quiz.explanation: Routine oxygen does not help patients with normal saturation.

options: A clinic for an outpatient stress test
Any hospital with a CT scanner
quiz.explanation: Target: first contact to device 90 minutes or less.

quiz.q: Who is most likely to have ACS without chest pain?
options: A smoker with typical pressure pain
quiz.explanation: Women, older adults and people with diabetes present atypically more often.

quiz.q: Which systolic BP rules out nitroglycerin?
quiz.explanation: Also heart rate below 50/min, RV infarction, or recent PDE-5 inhibitors.

flashcards.question: The three acute coronary syndromes
flashcards.answer: Unstable angina (no necrosis), NSTEMI (necrosis, no ST elevation), STEMI (complete occlusion, ST elevation).

flashcards.question: Aspirin in ACS
flashcards.answer: 162–325 mg, non-enteric, chewed. It blocks platelet aggregation; chewing speeds absorption.

flashcards.question: Nitroglycerin: when not to give
flashcards.answer: Systolic BP below 90 mmHg, heart rate below 50/min, suspected RV infarction, sildenafil or vardenafil within 24 hours, tadalafil within 48 hours.

flashcards.question: STEMI destination
flashcards.answer: Straight to a PCI-capable centre with pre-notification; first contact to device 90 minutes or less.

flashcards.question: OPQRST
flashcards.answer: Onset, Provocation/Palliation, Quality, Region/Radiation, Severity, Time.

flashcards.question: Why diabetics may have ACS without pain
flashcards.answer: Nerve damage blunts cardiac pain; they present with breathlessness, nausea, fatigue or confusion.

flashcards.question: Non-modifiable risk factors
flashcards.answer: Age (men 45 or older, women 55 or older), male sex, family history of premature coronary disease.

flashcards.question: Oxygen for every chest pain?
flashcards.answer: No. Give it if SpO₂ is below 90% or the patient is short of breath.

critical.scenario: A 58-year-old has "an elephant on my chest" radiating to the jaw, pale and sweaty. BP 142/88, HR 104, SpO₂ 97%. He takes tadalafil and took it yesterday.
critical.question: Best sequence?

options.t: Aspirin chewed, no nitroglycerin, no oxygen (saturation normal), 12-lead and PCI centre with pre-notification
options.f: Correct. Tadalafil within 48 hours rules out nitrates.

options.t: Aspirin and nitroglycerin: the interaction is minor
options.f: It can cause severe, hard-to-treat hypotension.

options.t: High-flow oxygen for all chest pain

options.f: A likely STEMI should go to PCI.

critical.explanation: Aspirin is safe; the PDE-5 inhibitor only rules out the nitrate.
critical.kpi: Applies contraindication knowledge for nitrate administration and prioritizes aspirin

critical.scenario: A 65-year-old woman with diabetes has had nausea, indigestion and unusual fatigue for 2 hours. No chest pain. BP 106/70, HR 108, cool and slightly sweaty.
critical.question: Interpretation and plan?

options.t: Possible atypical ACS: aspirin, 12-lead and emergency transport
options.f: Correct. No pain doesn't rule out ACS.

options.t: No chest pain, so not cardiac: routine transport
options.f: Diabetes and female sex make painless ACS likelier.
Sweating and tachycardia with risk factors need a 12-lead.
Don't explain away "indigestion" in a high-risk patient.

critical.explanation: Women, older adults and people with diabetes often present without chest pain.
critical.kpi: Recognizes atypical ACS presentation in high-risk populations (diabetics, women)

critical.scenario: A 52-year-old has ST elevation in V1–V4. A non-PCI hospital is 8 minutes away; a PCI centre is 28 minutes away. Your protocol allows bypass up to 30 minutes.
critical.question: Destination?

options.f: Correct. Going straight to PCI beats a stop and transfer.

options.t: The closer hospital: closer is always better
options.f: A transfer adds time to reperfusion.

options.t: Treat on scene until the pain settles

options.f: Explain why the PCI centre is the right choice.

critical.explanation: First contact to device should be 90 minutes or less; a stop at a non-PCI hospital usually blows that target.
critical.kpi: Applies STEMI destination protocols and understands the importance of primary PCI over secondary transfer
